text: Music therapy for children & Adolescents Dr. Smatya Wathawathana, Music therapist
A QUICK REVIEW Music therapy involves a trained and certified professional using music in a clinical and evidence- based way to accomplish each patient’s individualized objective.

Goals in music therapy to Promote - to promote wellness - to enhance attention span - to improve communication skills to Maintain - to maintain physical movement - to manage stress - to express feelings to Reduce - to reduce agitation - to alleviate pain - to reduce inappropriate behaviour

Children with special needs Special needs is an umbrella term for a wide array of diagnoses, from those that resolve quickly to those that will be a challenge for life and those that are relatively mild to those that are profound.

Music therapy for children with special needs Music therapy has long been valued as an important therapeutic and educational tool in the treatment of these diagoses as listed below -Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) - Intellectual Disabilities (ID) - Speech and Language Disorders - Physical Disabling Conditions - Developmental Delay - Emotional disturbance - Hospitalized child

benefits of music therapy for children Music therapy can have benefits such as: Pain management Normal growth and development Physical rehabilitation Opportunities for choice and control Anxiety and stress reduction Positive change in mood and emotional states Self expression Learning coping skills and techniques Family support Effect positive physiological changes Relaxation
benefits of music therapy for children (COnt.) Sharing music instruments playing music together Echo, Match the sound session seating start/stop Greeting songs, mirror dance Passing instruments

Music therapy session Although every music therapy sessions is different, here are some examples of common experiences and techniques by age group. Music therapy for infants is typically aimed at relaxation or developmental stimulation goals. Music therapy may reduce stress in infants, increasing oxygen saturation and lowering heart and breathing rate. When interacting with an infant, a music therapistinfants might: Sing or hum softly to baby Adapt music to be appropriate for infants who are able to tolerate only minimal levels of stimulation Play a reverie harp or guitar Encourage family involvement through singing Use a variety of interactive percussion along, rocking their baby instruments and songbooks to encourage reaching, grasping, visual attention and Teach families how to use music to encourage interaction growth and development

Music therapy for school-age kids can be similar to interventions provided for younger children, but older children may be able to engage in more complexSchool-age interventions, such as songwriting A school-aged child may be able to engage in projects which take more than one session to complete, such as free improvisation writing and recording an original song or learning a simple song on the guitar or xylophone guided relaxation techniques These interventions can promote mastery and self-esteem as well as encourage involvement in their society.

Music therapy for adolescents can be helpful for actively processing feelings and emotions associated with illness, developing techniques to cope with anxiety and pain, and providing normative musicaladolescents experiences. Adolescents may engage in: Songwriting Creation of playlists to promote mood change Lyric analysis to promote emotional processing, relaxation or movement goals Guided relaxation and learn techniques to be used outside of the music therapy session

a case study of jonah For one young man, music therapy changed his life. Music Therapy expert Kat Fulton describes the obstacles and achievements that Jonah, completely blind child- born without eyes. He was a preemie born at 21 weeks and adopted by his family. Before Jonah started music therapy he was unable to read braille and could not cope with difficult tasks. Through working with his music therapist and using his natural affinity for music, he has started learning how to read, vocalizing two to three words at a time – dramatically increasing his communication skills. Beyond his improvement in language, and with the help of music, Jonah is able to stay calm in situations that would have previously frustrated him, such as learning to tie his shoes. Where other strategies have failed to yield progress, music therapy has succeeded in helping this child live a more fulfilling life.

Conclusion Music can be used throughout the child's day and in many ways. Music Therapy can be the therapy that supports and enhances the goals of all other therapies and treatments. The strategies and therapeutic benefits of music that are developed and facilitated can thereby enhance the whole child, as well as those who share in his or her world
